sub_answers.sub_question: Known limitations of SDP relaxations, including relaxation gap and infeasible rank conditions
sub_answers.text: The SDP relaxation can be exact, inexact, or even feasible while the original OPF instance is infeasible, demonstrating the possibility of a relaxation gap and pathological outcomes [d24659s0p0]. The presence of generation lower bounds can cause positive optimality gaps for SDP relaxations even in very small networks, indicating sensitivity to specific modeling constraints [d24659s0p0]. Exactness of SDP relaxations is closely tied to cone structure: cones that are rank-one generated (ROG) yield SDP exactness results, while failure of ROG conditions relates to infeasible rank conditions for exact recovery [d60142s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Nonconvexity, local minima, and global optimality issues associated with QCQP formulations
sub_answers.text: Quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) is computationally challenging and nonconvex, which complicates finding global optima and managing local minima [d106579s0p0]. Under genericity assumptions, optimizer coordinates are algebraic functions of input coefficients and the algebraic degree can be high, reflecting intrinsic complexity of global optimality conditions for QCQPs [d2055s0p0]. Reformulations and stationarity notions (e.g., P-stationarity) are required to characterize first- and second-order optimality and to enable specialized algorithms with favorable convergence properties [d106579s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Numerical stability and sensitivity to modeling errors for constrained least squares in radar
Trade-offs between model fidelity and computational tractability in choosing SDP versus QCQP
sub_answers.text: The QC relaxation preserves stronger links between voltage variables via convex envelopes and is theoretically stronger than the SOC relaxation, but it neither dominates nor is dominated by the SDP relaxation, indicating trade-offs in tightness versus formulation type [d26453s0p0]. Computationally, the QC and SOC relaxations tend to be significantly faster and more reliable than SDP relaxations with current solvers, offering a tractability advantage at some potential cost in tightness relative to SDP in certain cases [d26453s0p0]. In other application domains, manifold-based nonconvex methods can outperform SDP-based benchmarks at much lower computational complexity, illustrating a broader trade-off between model fidelity of convex relaxations and practical solver efficiency [d76687s0p0].

Typical performance metrics used to evaluate joint receiver and waveform design (SINR, detection probability)
sub_answers.text: Sidelobe and correlation metrics such as side lobe correlation level (SLCL) and peak side lobe ratio (PSLR) are used to evaluate waveform and filter joint designs [d81182s0p0]. Signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and system-level energy efficiency (EE) are used to assess joint transceiver or beamforming/waveform performance [d76687s0p0]. Mean-squared error (MSE), symbol error rate (SER), capacity-related low-SNR expressions, and reconstruction/error rates from denoising formulations are also typical performance metrics in such optimization studies [d21050s0p0] [d32544s0p0] [d43534s0p0] [d61455s0p0].

Common numerical algorithms used to solve constrained least squares problems
sub_answers.text: Krylov-subspace projection methods (implemented via Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization) and iterative solvers like LSQR/LSMR are commonly used for large-scale constrained least squares problems [d100164s0p0]. Operator-form decompositions that split a constrained least squares problem into components and then approximate each with Krylov methods are used to handle linear equality constraints without explicit null-space factorizations [d103964s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Interior-point and first-order methods for solving semidefinite programs
sub_answers.text: First-order methods on semidefinite matrix spaces include mirror-descent and stochastic mirror-descent variants that provide provable convergence rates and avoid solving a full SDP at each iteration [d49029s0p0]. Sequential semidefinite programming (SSP) generalizes SQP for nonlinear problems with semidefiniteness constraints and relies on semidefinite subproblems and careful symmetrization to exploit the PSD cone efficiently [d146523s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Typical solution approaches and relaxations for nonconvex QCQPs
sub_answers.text: Nonconvex QCQPs are typically relaxed by spectral methods (eigenvalue-based relaxations) or by semidefinite programming relaxations, with spectral methods being simple but loose and SDP relaxations being tighter but more computationally intensive [d18288s0p0]. Recent SDP formulations aim to retain the tight bound of conventional SDPs while enabling more efficient and scalable dual optimization approaches comparable in complexity to spectral methods [d18288s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Complexity classes and computational complexity of SDP versus QCQP solvers
Role of rank relaxation and eigenvalue decomposition in SDP and QCQP solution methods
sub_answers.text: Rank relaxation is used to convert rank-constrained problems into tractable convex relaxations, and specialized algorithms for low-rank least squares exploit recursive importance sketching and low-rank structure to reduce dimension and accelerate convergence [d63101s0p0]. Spectral (eigenvalue) relaxations play a role in QCQP and BQP approaches as eigen-decomposition based methods that are simple to implement but provide looser bounds compared with SDP relaxations [d18288s0p0]. Semidefinite methods explicitly handle the positive semidefinite cone and leverage eigenstructure in their symmetrization and subproblem formulations, linking eigenvalue behavior to the treatment of rank and PSD constraints [d146523s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Characterize specific failure modes of semidefinite programming relaxations: quantify typical relaxation gaps on benchmark QCQPs, conditions under which the relaxed solution lacks a rank‑one decomposition (failed rank recovery), examples where Slater’s condition or strong duality break down, and known sufficient/necessary algebraic criteria for exactness (e.g., PSD cone extreme point structure, eigenvalue multiplicity arguments).
sub_answers.text: A closed convex conic subset S of the PSD cone is rank-one generated (ROG) exactly when all its extreme rays are generated by rank-one matrices, and ROGness is closely related to exactness of SDP relaxations for related QCQPs [d60142s0p0]. [d60142s0p0] gives sufficient conditions that guarantee S is ROG when S is the intersection of the PSD cone with finitely many homogeneous linear matrix inequalities and conic constraints. In the special case of two linear matrix inequalities those sufficient conditions are also shown to be necessary, extending the explicit characterization available for the single-LMI (S-lemma) case [d60142s0p0]. The ROG framework can be translated into inhomogeneous SDP exactness results and convex hull descriptions for QCQPs, recovering known reformulations such as the perspective reformulation for a simple mixed-binary set [d60142s0p0].

sub_answers.text: The Quadratic Convex (QC) relaxation is stronger than the Second-Order Cone (SOC) relaxation but neither dominates nor is dominated by the Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxation, indicating trade-offs in tightness among these models [d26453s0p0]. Computational experiments show the QC relaxation can give significant accuracy improvements over SOC at a reasonable computational cost, especially when networks have tight bounds, implying QC can be a middle ground between SOC and SDP in practice [d26453s0p0]. Current SDP solvers are significantly slower and less reliable than QC and SOC solvers on realistic instances, so tighter SDP models can be intractable in practice while QC or SOC approximations are faster and more dependable [d26453s0p0]. Scalability techniques for SDP (randomized algorithms and entropy-penalized approaches) can drastically reduce storage and arithmetic costs or deliver nearly linear-time gradient iterations, which mitigates but does not eliminate the higher computational burden of SDP compared to simpler relaxations [d55114s0p0][d42341s0p0]. SDP relaxations can nonetheless be inexact or even yield feasible relaxations when the original problem is infeasible (in optimal power flow), highlighting cases where tighter SDP formulations do not guarantee correctness despite higher cost [d24659s0p0].

Provide a precise definition of 'constrained least squares' problems, list the most common types of constraints encountered (e.g., equality, inequality, linear, affine, box, norm, sparsity), and give brief examples of each
sub_answers.text: Cx = d for linear equality constraints [d103964s0p0]. Equality constraints appear as linear equations Cx = d in least-squares formulations [d103964s0p0]. Inequality and affine constraints (both equalities and inequalities) arise in control and optimization settings, e.g., stochastic linear-quadratic control with affine constraints uses both equality and inequality constraints [d81575s0p0]. Box constraints (componentwise bounds) and linear constraints appear in primal-dual and Hoffman-constant analyses of constrained feasibility and least-squares style problems [d91698s0p0]. Norm-based and sparsity-inducing constraints or regularizers (e.g., l1, group-lasso, decomposable norms) are used in regularized least squares to promote sparsity or structure [d26049s0p0]; explicit sparsity constraints also appear in quadratic programs aiming for sparse solutions [d78699s0p0]. Semi-infinite variants, where the design matrix has an infinite dimension, give an example of infinite-dimensional constrained least squares used in function approximation and learning (semi-infinite linear regression) [d66612s0p0].

List and compare numerical algorithms and solver frameworks used for constrained least-squares problems (e.g., Tikhonov/regularized LS, equality- and inequality-constrained LS): active-set methods, null-space and range-space elimination, projected gradient / projected conjugate gradient, trust-region reflective methods, Lagrange multiplier and KKT-based solvers, QR/SVD-based direct solvers, LSQR and CGLS iterative methods — include conditions when each is preferred, convergence rates, and numerical stability issues.
sub_answers.text: Lanczos bidiagonalization-based LSQR and its mathematically equivalent CGLS are commonly used for large-scale linear least-squares and have intrinsic regularizing effects where the iteration count k acts as a regularization parameter and leads to semi-convergence capturing dominant SVD components for severely and moderately ill-posed problems [d33881s0p0]. LSMR has similar regularizing effects to LSQR and is superior to CGME, and hybrid LSMR projects A onto a Krylov subspace and applies a regularization term to the projections while using LSQR to solve inner least-squares problems whose conditioning improves as k increases [d100164s0p0][d33881s0p0]. Equality-constrained least-squares (LSE) can be decomposed into two operator-form LS problems and solved by two Krylov-subspace iterative methods that avoid forming the nullspace or heavy matrix factorizations, making them suitable for large-scale constrained LS [d103964s0p0]. Null-space and range-space eliminations and orthogonal projections in constrained optimization can be implemented by a sparse QR factorization or by a preconditioned LSQR iteration, and exploiting reduced compact representations of inverse KKT structure can yield efficient search directions when the constraint Jacobian is sparse [d64743s0p0][d103964s0p0]. Encoding a priori information as a right preconditioner (e.g., Bayesian prior) changes the Krylov subspaces for CGLS and can determine the null-space contribution in underdetermined problems, improving practical solution quality [d26760s0p0].
